title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
hints: you don't need every value up front - you only need to know 'what's the smallest value not yet visited' at each step, and be able to advance past it cheaply
initialize by pushing every node from the root down along its leftmost path onto a stack - the top of the stack is now the smallest unvisited value
next pops the top of the stack (that's the answer) and then pushes that node's right child's entire leftmost path onto the stack, since that subtree is now the next place to look for smaller values
hasNext is just checking whether the stack is empty
simulate this process fresh for each test case, starting from an empty stack and the tree's root, processing the ops string token by token in order
commonMistakes: materializing the full inorder list up front (which works but doesn't reflect the O(h) space / amortized O(1) time the design is meant to teach)
forgetting to push the right child's leftmost path after popping a node in next, which breaks the traversal after the first right turn
pushing a node's right child directly without first walking down its own leftmost path, which skips smaller values in that subtree
confusing this tree's binary-search-tree ordering with a general binary tree and trying to compare values instead of relying purely on structure and inorder position

content.problemStatement:
Binary trees in these problems are encoded as a flat array named `tree` using complete-binary-tree (heap) indexing:

- the root sits at index 0
- a node at index `i` has its left child at index `2*i+1` and right child at index `2*i+2`
- a child index only counts as real if it's within the array bounds **and** its value isn't the sentinel `-101`, which means "no node there"

The given tree is always a valid binary search tree.

**Design an iterator that walks the tree's nodes in ascending (inorder) order, supporting `next` (returns the value of the next smallest node not yet returned, and advances past it) and `hasNext` (reports whether any node remains to be returned).**

Since this problem asks for a single pure function rather than a stateful object, you're given the tree plus a space-delimited string of operations (each token either "next" or "hasNext"). Simulate a freshly constructed iterator running through each operation in order, and return a list of results: the returned value for each "next", and 1 or 0 for each "hasNext".
constraints: the given tree always satisfies the binary search tree property
every "next" token in ops is only ever called when a preceding hasNext (implicit or checked) would have returned true
notes: a left-only or right-only chain, stressing how far the traversal state needs to reach before finding the next value
ops consisting entirely of hasNext calls with no next calls at all

sampleTestCases.input: tree = [7, 3, 15, -101, -101, 9, 20], ops = "next next hasNext next hasNext"
sampleTestCases.explanation: inorder order is 3, 7, 9, 15, 20; the first two next calls return 3 and 7, hasNext is true since 9, 15, 20 remain, next returns 9, and hasNext is still true since 15 and 20 remain
a single-node tree: hasNext is true before any calls, next returns the only value 1, and hasNext is false afterward since nothing remains
inorder order is 1, 2, 3; after three next calls every node has been returned, so the final hasNext is false

optimal.time: O(1) amortized per next call (O(h) worst case for a single call, but each node is pushed and popped exactly once across the whole run), O(1) for hasNext
optimal.space: O(h) for the stack, where h is the tree's height
optimal.pattern: stack-based lazy inorder traversal: keep only the path of left ancestors on a stack, expanding one step at a time

bruteForce.approach: do a full inorder traversal up front, collecting every value into a list, then serve next and hasNext calls by walking a plain index cursor through that precomputed list
bruteForce.time: O(n) up front, O(1) per operation after that
bruteForce.space: O(n) to store the entire traversal
